screens.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
screens.subtitle: Design so features are added by extension, not by changing proven code.

narration.text: Today we begin with a cornerstone of resilient design: the Open/Closed Principle. The claim is simple but powerful: software entities should be open for extension and closed for modification. That sounds like a paradox at first, so our goal is to make this idea concrete. You will learn what is meant by being 'open' and 'closed', why abstraction resolves the tension between them, and how common code patterns — especially sprawling conditional logic — lead to OCP violations. We'll use two short, practical examples: a payment processor that grows endless conditionals, and a discount calculator that needs new customer types. These examples illustrate the danger: changing tested code every time a new case appears increases regressions and technical debt. Throughout this lesson, notice how designing around abstractions—interfaces or contracts—lets you add new behaviors by adding new modules instead of touching old ones. By the end, you'll be able to recognize OCP violations, explain the safe alternative using abstractions, and apply simple refactor strategies to keep code stable while it evolves. Think about a recent bug you fixed: could that change have been added as an extension instead?

keyIdea.title: Why OCP matters
keyIdea.text: OCP reduces regressions by encouraging new behavior through added modules rather than changing tested code, using abstraction to keep systems stable and adaptable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Open/Closed Principle
Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
Open for extension, closed for modification — design to add behavior without editing stable code.
Stable base

Keep proven implementations intact to avoid regressions when requirements change.

Extend safely

Add new implementations that conform to an abstraction rather than editing existing code.

Core idea

Use interfaces or abstract contracts so the system can accept new behaviors via new types without changing the original implementation.

Explore Key Topics
Paradox & resolution, conditional-logic violations, and using abstraction for safe extension.
Paradox
What 'open' and 'closed' mean and why they are compatible via abstraction.
Violation pattern
Conditional logic that grows every time a new case is added.
Refactor approach
Depend on abstractions and add new implementations for new behaviors.
Visual concept
A base module depends on an abstraction. New concrete modules implement that abstraction. The base module remains unchanged as new behaviors are added.
Quick start
As you go through the chapter, identify if conditionals would need editing for each new requirement. If so, consider an abstraction-based refactor.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to precisely define the Open/Closed Principle, explain why it appears paradoxical, and resolve that paradox using abstraction. You will also be able to argue why OCP matters for stability and maintenance, and to spot common code patterns that break OCP — most notably, conditional logic that must be edited each time a new case appears. We will walk through examples that show both the violation and the safer design using an interface or abstract contract. Each objective links a concept to a practical skill: define the principle clearly, articulate its trade-offs, and identify code smells that signal an OCP problem. For learners who maintain codebases, these skills reduce regression risk and help plan safer refactors. You'll practice by analyzing starter code and describing how you would transform it so new behaviors are added by extension rather than modification. Keep in mind that OCP guides design choices; it does not forbid bug fixes or reasonable adjustments to existing, incorrect behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Detection
screens.subtitle: Apply OCP in code review, spot violations, and choose sensible abstractions

narration.text: This second objectives slide moves from description to action. You will practice identifying OCP violations in existing code and choosing refactors that replace conditional branching with extension points. The learning here is pragmatic: distinguish a genuine need for an abstraction from over-engineering. That means anticipating likely future changes but avoiding speculative complexity for unlikely scenarios. You will learn to balance risk: when frequent edits to the same method signal OCP violation, prefer introducing a small interface and concrete types. When changes are rare, a simpler approach may be acceptable. As part of the chapter you will analyze starter code that uses if-else chains to handle payment and discount types, describe how to modify it to obey OCP, and justify that design. These skills translate directly to safer maintenance: fewer regressions, easier testing of new behaviors in isolation, and clearer responsibilities across components. Finally, you will practice writing exam-style answers that explain why a given change violates or preserves OCP.

screens.title: What OCP Says — a precise definition
screens.subtitle: Open for extension, closed for modification — unpacking the words

narration.text: Let's define OCP in practical terms. The principle states that software entities — classes, modules, functions — should be open for extension but closed for modification. Open for extension means you can add new behaviors or functionality to a component when requirements change. Closed for modification means you should not have to edit the component's existing source code to introduce those behaviors. The tension between adding features and keeping existing code unchanged is resolved by using abstraction: a stable module should depend on a contract, not concrete implementations. That contract can be an interface or an abstract class. When a new behavior is required, we write a new implementation of the contract and plug it in, leaving the original module's code untouched. A concrete example: instead of editing a single method to handle a new payment type, define a payment method interface and implement a new class for the new type. A common misconception is that OCP forbids any change to existing code; it does not. Bug fixes may still require modification. The principle guides how to add new features safely. Key takeaway: design for likely change by defining clear contracts that let you add new modules instead of altering working ones.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: OCP prescribes adding new behavior through new modules that implement an abstraction, not by editing existing, tested code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Definition
Open/Closed — clear terms

Open for extension: add new behavior. Closed for modification: avoid editing established code. The two coexist via abstraction.

Abstraction

A contract (interface/abstract class) that lets multiple concrete types provide behavior without changing the dependent code.

Extension

Introduce new implementations to satisfy new requirements rather than edit existing ones.

Misconception

OCP does not ban all modifications. Bug fixes and reasonable refactors are allowed; OCP guides how to add new features.

Analogy: modular toy chassis

Imagine a toy car chassis that accepts new parts. You add new modules without altering the base frame. The chassis is closed; new parts make it open.

Key Takeaway

Design components to depend on stable contracts so features are added by creating new implementations rather than editing the component itself.

screens.title: How abstraction resolves the paradox
screens.subtitle: From editing logic to plugging in implementations

narration.text: This lesson walks through the practical steps to resolve the open/closed tension using abstraction. Start with an existing module that performs behavior directly — for example, processing different payment types inside a single method. Step one: identify the varying behaviors that change when requirements evolve. Step two: extract a small, focused abstraction that captures the behavior you depend on — for payments, a payment method contract. Step three: make the original module depend on that abstraction rather than concrete types. Step four: implement each behavior as a separate concrete class that adheres to the contract. Finally, wire new implementations into the system without editing the original module. A concrete scenario: a payment processor currently uses a string switch to decide which processing routine to run. After refactor, the processor accepts a payment method interface and calls a single method like execute or pay. To add ApplePay, implement the interface and register it. A common mistake is to create a huge, generic abstraction that tries to cover every possible future case; keep the contract minimal and focused. This process reduces the risk of regressions while enabling new functionality through extension. Ask yourself: which behaviors in your codebase change most often and could be modelled as plug-ins?

keyIdea.title: Refactor steps
keyIdea.text: Identify variable behavior, extract a focused contract, depend on abstraction, add concrete implementations for new features.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Process Flow
Resolve the paradox — four steps
1
Find varying behavior

Look for code that changes when new types appear.

2
Define a contract

Extract a minimal interface capturing the behavior your module needs.

3
Depend on abstraction

Make the original module accept the interface instead of concrete cases.

4
Add implementations

Implement each behavior separately and register or inject as needed.

Concrete scenario

A payment processor using if-else branches is refactored to depend on a payment method interface. Adding ApplePay becomes adding an implementation rather than editing the processor.

Common pitfall

Avoid creating broad abstractions that try to foresee every future need. Keep interfaces focused on the actual variation points.

screens.title: Why OCP increases stability and reduces regressions
screens.subtitle: Comparing edit-every-time vs extend-by-adding approaches

narration.text: This lesson compares two maintenance models and explains why the OCP approach reliably increases stability. Model A modifies existing code whenever a new requirement arrives. Each change risks regressions because established, tested logic is altered. Model B defines an abstraction and adds new modules that implement that abstraction. When you add new modules, you introduce new code which can be tested independently and does not change the behavior of existing modules. Practically, Model B yields several benefits: existing functionality remains intact and less likely to break, tests for the original module still pass, and the cognitive load on maintainers is lower because new responsibilities are in newly added files. For example, a reporting system that branches on format will require edits for every new format under Model A. Under Model B, each format is a separate implementation that the report generator accepts through an interface. A common misunderstanding is thinking Model B always requires more files and more complexity; it does require additional modules, but this tradeoff is worthwhile when the change surface is frequent. The rule of thumb: when you expect ongoing addition of cases, prefer extension to modification. Ask: which of your subsystems change often enough to justify separate implementations?

keyIdea.title: Stability vs change
keyIdea.text: Adding new modules keeps tested behavior intact and isolates risk; editing core code increases regression risk and cognitive overhead.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Comparison
Model A — Edit every time

You add branches or cases inside existing methods. Each addition edits tested logic and increases regression risk.

  • • Requires modifying core code for each new type.
  • • Tests for the original method may need updates.
  • • Cognitive overhead rises as logic grows.
Model B — Extend by adding

Define a contract and create new implementations for each behavior. The base module remains unchanged and stable.

  • • New behavior is added as new modules.
  • • Existing tests remain meaningful and passing.
  • • Easier to test and reason about new code in isolation.
Benefit
Reduced regressions
Tradeoff
More files, clearer responsibilities
Guideline
Refactor when changes are frequent

screens.title: PaymentProcessor: an OCP violation example
screens.subtitle: A single method with conditional branches that grows with new payment types

narration.text: Now we examine a concrete example taken from the chapter: a PaymentProcessor class that decides handling based on a payment type string and a sequence of conditionals. This pattern violates OCP because adding any new payment type requires editing a central, working method. Consider the consequences: every addition risks breaking existing flows and forces retesting of the original logic. The better design is to depend on a payment method abstraction and add new concrete implementations for each payment type. In the example code, separate private methods handle credit card, PayPal, and bank transfers, but the processPayment method contains the branching logic. That central switch is the problem. A misconception is to think that using private helper methods alone solves the issue; it does not. The key is to remove the decision point from the class's implementation and accept a polymorphic payment object instead. Visualize the refactor: processPayment calls a single method on a payment interface. Adding ApplePay becomes creating a new class that implements that interface, not editing the processor. This reduces risk and makes the code base extensible and testable in isolation. How many places in your code use string switches to decide behavior?

keyIdea.title: Payment example
keyIdea.text: A central conditional dispatcher forces modifications for each new type; prefer a payment method interface and concrete implementations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Code Walkthrough
Original pattern (violates OCP)
<!-- Java-like pseudocode shown as provided -->
public class PaymentProcessor {
    public void processPayment(String paymentType, double amount) {
        if ("CreditCard".equals(paymentType)) {
            processCreditCardPayment(amount);
        } else if ("PayPal".equals(paymentType)) {
            processPayPalPayment(amount);
        } else if ("BankTransfer".equals(paymentType)) {
            processBankTransferPayment(amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Unsupported payment type: " + paymentType);
        }
    }

    private void processCreditCardPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
    private void processPayPalPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
    private void processBankTransferPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
}
Why this breaks OCP
  • • Adding a new payment type requires editing processPayment.
  • • Existing, tested logic is modified, increasing regression risk.
  • • The class centralizes decision logic and violates single responsibility for behavior extension.
Concrete fix (concept)
Introduce a PaymentMethod interface and implement concrete classes. Let PaymentProcessor accept a PaymentMethod and call a single method to execute payment logic.

screens.title: Abstraction: the mechanism that makes OCP practical
screens.subtitle: Interfaces and abstract classes as contracts for extension

narration.text: Abstraction is the tool that makes the Open/Closed Principle achievable. A contract defines the operations a dependent module requires without prescribing how those operations are implemented. When a module is written against a contract, new behaviors can be added by supplying new concrete types that fulfill the contract. Importantly, the contract should be minimal and focused on the variation point. Overly broad contracts invite complexity and coupling. For example, if a payment contract only needs a single method to execute a payment, adding dozens of unrelated methods to the interface would make every implementation heavier and harder to change. A practical guideline is to extract the smallest useful interface that supports the original module's needs. Another misconception is to think abstraction always means heavy frameworks or patterns; often a small interface and dependency injection suffice. The result of correct abstraction is that the core module's code does not change when new types are added, and new types can be tested in isolation. Ask yourself: what are the smallest operations your module depends on, and can those be specified as a simple contract?

keyIdea.title: Abstraction is minimal
keyIdea.text: Create focused contracts describing required operations so new implementations can be added without changing the dependent code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Definition
Abstraction as contract

Define only the operations a client requires. New implementations provide behavior without changing the client.

Do

Keep interfaces small and focused on variation points.

Don't

Create huge abstractions that anticipate every hypothetical future need.

Analogy

A power socket is a small contract: any appliance that fits the socket can draw power without the socket changing.

screens.title: Frequent OCP violations and how to spot them
screens.subtitle: If-else chains, switches, and scattered type checks

narration.text: This lesson highlights the common patterns that often indicate an OCP violation and gives practical detection tips. The most common smell is a long chain of conditional statements that dispatch behavior based on a type or string. These typically live inside a single method and grow whenever a new case must be handled. Another smell is duplicated branching logic across multiple classes — when the same decision appears in many places, it's a sign that behavior should be centralized behind an abstraction. A third pattern is tightly-coupled type checks, where code inspects concrete types to pick behavior. To spot violations during code review, ask: does adding a new case require changing this method or adding a new module? If it requires a change, that's an OCP candidate for refactor. Also look for comments like 'add more cases here' which often signal brittle design. A common misconception is to treat these refactors as purely structural; they are design decisions that affect testability, deployment, and team velocity. When you find a smell, prefer a small, focused interface and move behavior into dedicated implementations. The diagnostic question to carry forward is: can I add this behavior without editing the tested code?

keyIdea.title: Smells to watch
keyIdea.text: Long conditional chains, duplicated dispatch logic, and type-checking branches often indicate an OCP violation and an opportunity for abstraction.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Common Mistakes
If-else chains

Long chains that require editing when new cases arrive.

Duplicated dispatch

Same decision logic repeated in multiple places instead of a single abstraction.

Type checks

Inspecting concrete types to decide behavior couples callers to implementations.

Quick detection checklist
  • • Will adding a new type require editing this method?
  • • Is dispatch logic duplicated across files?
  • • Are concrete types inspected to choose behavior?

screens.title: DiscountCalculator activity — identify the violation
screens.subtitle: Analyze the starter code and explain how it violates OCP

narration.text: Now apply what you've learned to the DiscountCalculator starter code from the chapter. The class calculates discounts based on a customer type string and uses if-else blocks to set discount percentages. This forces modification whenever a new customer type needs a discount rate. The activity asks you to run the main program to observe current behavior and then imagine adding a new type like 'Loyalty' at twelve percent. To accommodate that change the existing method must be edited, which demonstrates the violation of 'closed for modification.' The correct approach is to extract a DiscountPolicy interface with a method that computes discount given a purchase amount. Each customer type becomes a concrete implementation: StandardPolicy, PremiumPolicy, VIPPolicy, and LoyaltyPolicy. A dispatcher or registry selects the appropriate policy instance; the calculator uses the policy interface rather than branching on strings. This structure keeps the DiscountCalculator unchanged when new policies are added. Common learner mistakes include creating a single monolithic Policy with flags for types — that recreates branching internally. Instead, prefer separate classes that each implement the single behavior. As you work through the activity, describe the edits required and why they break OCP, then propose the minimal contract that prevents future modifications.

keyIdea.title: Activity focus
keyIdea.text: Identify how the DiscountCalculator's conditional logic forces modification and propose a small DiscountPolicy abstraction to allow extension.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Hands-on Activity
Starter code (excerpt)
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public double calculateDiscount(String customerType, double purchaseAmount) {
        double discount = 0;

        if ("Standard".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.05; // 5% for standard customers
        } else if ("Premium".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.10; // 10% for premium customers
        } else if ("VIP".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.15; // 15% for VIP customers
        } else {
            // no specific discount
        }
        return discount;
    }
}
Analysis prompt
  • • Run the main program to observe current outputs for Standard, Premium, and VIP.
  • • Imagine adding 'Loyalty' at 12%: how would you change this code?
  • • Explain why that change violates OCP's closed-for-modification requirement.
Suggested refactor
Create DiscountPolicy interface and separate classes per customer type. Inject or select a policy instance instead of branching on strings.

narration.text: This screen presents a simple architecture pattern that enforces OCP: a stable core module depends on a contract, and concrete implementations provide behavior. The pattern has three components: the contract, the core module that depends on the contract, and concrete implementations for each behavior. The core module receives the contract via constructor injection, a registry, or a factory that returns an instance based on configuration. When a new behavior is required, add a new implementation and update wiring or registration; the core module's source stays unchanged. For example, a report generator depends on ReportFormat interface. Each format — PDF, CSV, Excel — is a class that implements the interface. The report generator simply calls a standard method to render output. Important considerations: keep the contract minimal; design for testability by unit testing each implementation in isolation; and make wiring explicit so adding a new implementation does not implicitly change behavior at runtime. A frequent error is to hide logic in the factory and keep branching there; while this centralizes dispatch, it still requires modification when new types are added. Prefer pluggable registration or dependency injection so registration changes are confined and auditable. The core insight: moving decision points to configuration and new modules preserves the closed nature of the core.

keyIdea.title: Architecture pattern
keyIdea.text: Core depends on contract; implementations supply behavior. Wire implementations without editing the core logic to preserve OCP.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Architecture
Contract

A minimal interface that defines the operation the core requires.

Core module

Depends on the contract and invokes a single method to perform behavior.

Implementations

Each behavior is a concrete class that implements the contract and can be added without editing the core.

Wiring options
  • • Constructor injection: pass the implementation to the core during creation.
  • • Registry or plugin registration: register implementations so the system selects them without changing core logic.
  • • Factory with configuration: factory returns appropriate implementation, but minimize branching in the factory.

screens.title: Common-problem checklist and quick refactor recipe
screens.subtitle: A short workflow to decide if and how to apply OCP

narration.text: This slide provides a practical checklist and a concise refactor recipe to apply in code reviews. Start with the checklist: does adding a new case require modifying an existing method? Is dispatch logic duplicated? Are concrete types inspected to choose behavior? If you answer yes, consider the refactor. The recipe has three steps: first, identify the variation point — the place behavior diverges. Second, design a minimal contract expressing just what the client needs. Third, implement current cases as separate classes and replace branching with dependency on the contract. Test each new implementation in isolation and then integrate it. A useful intermediate strategy is to introduce a registry or small factory so new implementations can be registered without rewriting code. Remember to avoid over-engineering: apply this pattern when changes are likely and frequent. A common misconception is to use this pattern everywhere; that increases complexity unnecessarily. When changes are truly rare, the cost-benefit may favor a smaller, localized change. Use the checklist as a pragmatic decision tool: if edits are frequent, refactor; if edits are rare, measure the cost and decide accordingly. End by asking: which three methods in your current project are edited most often and might benefit from this recipe?

keyIdea.title: Refactor recipe
keyIdea.text: Detect variation, extract minimal contract, implement new classes, and test implementations in isolation before integrating.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Check Your Understanding
Checklist
  • • Will adding a new case edit this method?
  • • Is dispatch logic duplicated across modules?
  • • Do tests break when new cases are added?
Refactor recipe
  1. Identify the variation point.
  2. Extract a minimal contract for the behavior.
  3. Create concrete implementations and wire them via injection or registration.
  4. Test implementations and keep the core unchanged.
Pro tip
Prefer focused contracts and explicit wiring. Avoid hiding branching in a central factory unless registration and plugin patterns are available.

screens.title: Practice questions and sample explanations
screens.subtitle: Verify understanding of OCP and its implications

narration.text: To consolidate learning, work through a short assessment in two parts. First, answer the multiple-choice questions provided in the chapter. One asks what 'closed for modification' means; the correct understanding is that new functionality should be added by extending behavior rather than altering existing code. Another asks about a report generator needing Excel support and whether adding Excel violates OCP if the generator uses branching; it does violate OCP because it requires modifying existing code. Second, practice explaining the reasoning in one or two sentences: for any given example, state which part is the variation point, what contract you would extract, and how a new implementation would be wired. When writing explanations, emphasize the tangible benefits: fewer regressions, easier testing, and clearer separation of responsibilities. A common pitfall in student answers is to confuse OCP with never changing code; remind yourself that bug fixes and logical corrections still require edits — OCP only prescribes how to introduce new behavior. Use these assessment prompts to practice concise justifications you could use in code reviews or design documents. Practice questions and sample explanations means practice answering why an example violates or preserves ocp, focusing on variation points, contracts, and benefits of extension.. In practical terms, verify understanding of ocp and its implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Assessment prompts
Multiple choice

Which statement matches 'closed for modification' in OCP? Correct answer: add new functionality by extending behaviour rather than altering existing code.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Let's summarize three ideas you should carry forward. First, the Open/Closed Principle asks that systems be open to extension but closed to modification; this protects stable code and reduces regressions. Second, abstraction — small, focused interfaces or abstract classes — is the practical mechanism that resolves the apparent paradox by separating contracts from implementations. Third, the most common violation is conditional dispatch: if-else or switch logic that must be changed whenever a new type is added. When you detect these smells, prefer extracting a minimal contract and adding new, testable implementations. Avoid over-engineering by designing contracts for likely change, not for every hypothetical future. These three points will help you evaluate when a refactor is necessary and how to implement it safely. Ask yourself: what three places in your codebase would benefit from this approach?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: OCP protects stability by adding new code for new behavior; use focused abstractions and watch for conditional dispatch as the main violation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Open/Closed Principle

Software entities should be open to extension but closed to modification to prevent regressions.

Abstraction

Use minimal interfaces or abstract classes so new functionality is added via implementations.

Conditional logic

If-else and switch statements that expand for new types are a primary sign of OCP violation.

Takeaway

Prefer adding new modules over editing old ones. Use focused contracts and test new implementations in isolation.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to reference during development

narration.text: A final quick reference to use in your daily work: First, remember the phrasing 'open for extension, closed for modification' — it guides how you add new behavior. Second, prefer small interfaces or contracts to capture the behavior the core needs; keep them focused. Third, watch for sprawling conditionals and duplicated dispatch logic; these are the most common signs that a refactor toward OCP is needed. When in doubt, ask whether a feature can be added without changing existing, tested code. If not, consider extracting a contract and adding a new implementation. These short rules help you make measured design decisions that improve stability and reduce maintenance costs over time. Keep them on a sticky note near your editor during code reviews. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means phrase, pattern, and smell: ocp phrasing, use small contracts, and watch for conditional dispatch as the key violation.. In practical terms, three compact cards to reference during development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick Reference
keyIdea.text: Phrase, pattern, and smell: OCP phrasing, use small contracts, and watch for conditional dispatch as the key violation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Quick Reference
Phrase

Open for extension, closed for modification.

Pattern

Depend on a small contract; add implementations for new behavior.

Smell

Expanding if-else or switch statements that handle new types.

Final takeaway

Design for extension where change is likely. Add new modules, keep the core closed and tested.
